headline: Trump extends $100,000 H-1B payment proclamation 12 months to September 21, 2027 — while fee stays blocked by court order
label: Sep 19, 2026
source: White House / Mint / LatestLY / IANS
summary: President Trump signed a proclamation on September 18, 2026, extending the 2025 $100,000 H-1B payment requirement another 12 months, until 12:00 a.m. EDT on September 21, 2027. The White House says registrations from the largest IT staffing/outsourcing firms fell 92% since the payment and weighted-selection system took effect, more than 700 petitions included the $100,000 payment, and FY2027 registrations shifted toward higher-paid, advanced-degree workers (US master's+ share rose from 45.1% to 66.1%). Limited national-interest exceptions remain. Critical distinction: the fee's enforceability is separate from the renewal — a federal court vacated the original proclamation (June 2026, upheld by the First Circuit in July), and Fragomen/immigration firms say the vacatur order should continue to prevent collection unless the legal position changes. This proclamation is distinct from DHS's separate proposed $103,265 H-1B rulemaking (Aug 25, 2026). Indians made up ~71% of approved H-1B petitions in FY2024, so the renewal signals prolonged pressure on Indian hiring even as collection is on hold.

label: Sep 18, 2026
headline: USCIS sweeping new public charge guidance takes effect — any means-tested benefits (SNAP, Medicaid, housing aid) now weigh against green card applicants
summary: USCIS’s new public charge policy guidance takes effect September 18, 2026, replacing the narrower 2022 standard. Officers may now consider receipt of any means-tested public benefit on or after September 18 — including SNAP, Medicaid/CHIP/WIC, public or assisted housing, and federal rental assistance — when deciding whether an applicant is ‘more likely than not’ to become dependent on government support for basic needs, a lower threshold than the 2022 rule’s ‘primarily dependent’ test. Benefits received before September 18 are judged only under the old standard (cash assistance like SSI/TANF and long-term institutionalization). The assessment remains a totality-of-the-circumstances test weighing five mandatory factors (age, health, family status, assets/resources, education/skills). Which standard applies depends on filing date, not decision date; the new Form I-485 edition is mandatory for applications filed on or after September 18, with older editions rejected. The rule covers EB-1/EB-2/EB-3 and immigrant investor applicants — the categories dominated by Indians transitioning from H-1B status — as well as family-sponsored and Diversity Visa applicants. Exemptions include refugees, asylees, VAWA/U/T holders, and existing green card holders renewing 10-year cards.
source: USCIS / Murthy Law Firm / Reddy Neumann Brown PC / LatestLY

headline: New executive order: State, Labor, DHS must weigh employer layoffs when reviewing H-1B cases — DOL gets 30 days to start retroactive LCA data review
label: Sep 18, 2026
source: White House / LatestLY / India Today / IANS
summary: President Trump signed an executive order on September 18, 2026, directing the Secretaries of State, Labor, and Homeland Security to consider — in labor condition applications, petitions, visa adjudications, and entry decisions — whether the sponsoring employer has directly or indirectly laid off similarly situated US workers in the previous year or plans future layoffs affecting them. A layoff does not automatically reject an H-1B case; it becomes a factor in review. The order also gives the DOL Wage and Hour Division 30 days to begin reviewing already-submitted LCA data to decide whether action under INA 212(n)(2)(G) is warranted against sponsors, and requires the three departments to consult Commerce, Education, and the SBA for wage, employment, academic, and industry data in H-1B processing. The White House purpose section claims tech employers sought H-1B workers while laying off 800,000–1.3 million Americans from 2022–2026. Signed the same day as the $100,000 proclamation renewal, the order adds a new employer-conduct dimension to H-1B adjudication with direct relevance to Indian professionals, the largest H-1B beneficiary group.

headline: State Department expands social media vetting to I, TN, TD visas effective Oct 1, 2026
label: Sep 18, 2026
source: US State Department / Envoy Global / VisaVerge / Indian Eagle
summary: The State Department announced on September 18, 2026, that its online presence (social media) review will expand to three more nonimmigrant visa categories effective October 1, 2026: I visas (foreign media representatives), TN visas (USMCA professionals), and TD visas (TN dependents). Applicants in these categories will be instructed to set all social media profiles to 'public' or 'open' for consular vetting. The change broadens screening that already applies to H-1B, F-1, M-1, J-1, K and other categories; it does not create a new visa category or change eligibility requirements. The I visa has the most direct relevance for Indian applicants (foreign journalists and media representatives traveling to the US for professional work); TN/TD mostly concern Canadian and Mexican nationals under the USMCA.

headline: Judge blocks Duration of Status rule one day before it takes effect — nationwide preliminary injunction, D/S framework stays
label: Sep 14, 2026
source: Reuters / Inside Higher Ed / Presidents' Alliance / U.S. District Court, D. Mass.
summary: U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV granted nationwide preliminary relief on September 14, 2026, blocking the DHS final rule that would have ended 'duration of status' for F-1/J-1 students and I-visa journalists on September 15. In a 48-page order in Presidents' Alliance et al. v. DHS, the judge barred DHS and ICE from implementing the rule while the APA challenge proceeds, writing that the government's national security rationale 'borders on the absurd' and was based on a handful of anecdotes the rule would do nothing to prevent. The court found DHS failed to respond to 22,000+ public comments, did not consider less restrictive alternatives, and estimated the harm to US higher education and the economy could be 'catastrophic.' The longstanding open-ended duration-of-status framework remains in place nationwide while the lawsuit continues, with further hearings set for October 2. Relief for Indian students, the largest international cohort in the US, especially PhD candidates whose programs exceed the proposed four-year cap.

label: Sep 11, 2026
headline: Federal Register publishes proposed rule to eliminate 60-day grace period — 60-day public comment period opens
summary: DHS published the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (RIN 1615-AD22) in the Federal Register on September 11, 2026, formally proposing to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, E-1/E-2/E-3, and TN workers after job loss, plus their dependents. This moves the rule from White House OMB clearance (Aug 31) to the actual public comment phase — 60 days for public input before DHS can issue a final rule. The NPRM discloses new details: about 3,795 workers use the grace period each year, 99.2% of them H-1B holders; DHS identified no direct benefits for workers or employers, acknowledged workers could lose wages and families could face sudden relocation costs, and conceded USCIS would have to spend resources placing non-departing workers into deportation proceedings, generating more work for ICE and backlogged immigration courts. Economist Daniel Di Martino (Manhattan Institute) warned the rule would give companies greater leverage over workers and steer them away from high-turnover startups, 'against the president's agenda of reducing abuse of the H-1B program.' The grace period remains fully in effect during the rulemaking process; it cannot end until a final rule is published.
source: Reuters / Federal Register (Doc. 2026-18631) / USA Today / Envoy Global

label: Sep 9, 2026
headline: Judge Saylor signals he may block Duration of Status rule before Sept 15 effective date — 'sceptical, at best' of national security rationale
summary: U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV signaled he may halt the DHS rule ending 'duration of status' before it takes effect September 15, telling the court he wants to rule before that date and could temporarily block the policy if more time is needed. At the September 3 hearing in the lawsuit brought by NAFSA, the Presidents' Alliance, AFT, UAW, and The NewsGuild-CWA, the judge appeared 'sceptical, at best' of DHS's national security justification: 'I am just struggling to see a rational connection — a four-year cap does not have anything to do with national security.' He dismissed the government's cited fraud cases as anecdotal and agreed DHS did not meaningfully respond to 22,000+ public comments, suggesting the government was 'trying to push this through at high speed rather than taking the comments of the affected communities seriously.' Unless blocked, the rule replaces open-ended duration of status with four-year fixed caps for F-1/J-1 students and 240-day caps for I-visa journalists starting September 15. NAFSA forecasts a 10% drop in international enrollment this year, costing the US economy $3.4 billion.
source: The PIE News / Boston Globe / NAFSA

headline: DHS interim final rule lets U.S.-born children of foreign government employees register as green card holders — implements birthright EO 14418
label: Sep 9, 2026
source: DHS / Federal Register / Law Offices of Keshab Raj Seadie
summary: DHS published an interim final rule (91 Fed. Reg. 57249, Docket USCIS-2026-0496) creating a mechanism for U.S.-born children of foreign government employees who do not acquire U.S. citizenship at birth under Executive Order 14418 to voluntarily register as lawful permanent residents. It broadens the existing framework — previously limited to children of accredited diplomatic officers — to cover nationals employed by their country's embassy or consulate, foreign government employees in official capacity, and qualifying international-organization employees. Published September 9, 2026, effective September 4, 2026, applying prospectively to children born on or after that date; Forms I-485 and G-325R are being revised. Comments accepted through October 5, 2026. Relevant to foreign diplomatic families in the US, including Indian diplomats.

label: Sep 8, 2026
headline: US resumes immigrant visa processing for Hungary and Poland — global pause remains elsewhere, India applicants report cancellations through September
summary: The Trump administration resumed processing immigrant visa applications from Hungary and Poland last week while keeping the temporary global pause in place at all other missions, according to four people familiar with the matter cited by Reuters. The directive to prioritize the two countries reportedly came from the White House. The State Department's August 25 global pause — ordered days after federal judges struck down the administration's 75-country blanket immigrant visa suspension — halted interviews worldwide pending mandatory 'public charge' training for consular officers. Applicants in India and elsewhere have posted about canceled interviews stretching through September. The pause could last months: posts must self-train on Washington-sent materials, then a consular officer must visit each mission to certify completion. The White House and State Department declined to explain why Hungary and Poland were singled out.
source: Reuters

headline: DOL suspends Cognizant's (and Cloudera's) PERM filings amid visa fraud probe — White House Fraud Task Force involved
label: Sep 8, 2026
source: DOL Inspector General (X) / PTI / The Hindu BusinessLine / Dainik Jagran / Outlook Business
summary: Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced on X on September 8 that Cognizant's PERM (Permanent Labor Certification) filings are suspended while investigators examine alleged fraud involving the H-1B and PERM programs, acting after 'multiple tips about violations from whistleblowers.' Cloudera's PERM filings were suspended the same day. The probe is being conducted alongside the White House Fraud Task Force and DOL is 'running down' prior applications one by one. DOL has not specified the allegations, the number of applications affected, or how long the suspension will last; it does not establish that fraud occurred. PERM is the first step of employment-based green card sponsorship — the suspension blocks Cognizant from starting new green card cases for foreign workers, raising concerns for the Chennai-founded IT major's Indian workforce and, per analysts, for the broader Indian IT sector's ability to attract and retain foreign talent on long-term US projects.

headline: State Department bars 'visa shopping': NIV applicants must interview in country of nationality or residence, effective immediately
label: Sep 6, 2026
source: US State Department / Mint
summary: The US State Department updated its instructions on September 6, 2026, requiring all nonimmigrant visa applicants to schedule their interview appointments at the US Embassy or Consulate in their country of nationality or legal residence, effective immediately. Nationals of countries where the US does not conduct routine NIV operations must apply at a designated post. The change shuts down a widely used workaround for Indian applicants, who during long backlogs booked B1/B2 and other NIV interviews at posts outside India (e.g., Bangkok) for faster slots. Indian nationals can no longer secure quicker appointments in other countries. Limited exceptions exist for designated locations where routine NIV processing is not conducted.

label: Sep 3, 2026
headline: Court hears arguments on Duration of Status injunction — ruling pending, rule still on track for September 15
summary: U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV heard oral arguments on September 3 in the lawsuit seeking to block the Duration of Status rule before its September 15 effective date (Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration et al. v. DHS, No. 1:26-cv-13799). The coalition of eight higher education and labor organizations — including NAFSA, the Presidents' Alliance, AFT, UAW, and The NewsGuild-CWA — argued DHS violated the Administrative Procedure Act by failing to conduct thorough impact analysis, not substantively responding to 22,000+ negative public comments, and not considering alternatives. Plaintiffs called the harms 'serious and irreparable' to international students, scholars, higher education institutions, the economy, and U.S. research. DHS had dismissed the lawsuit as 'performative outrage.' No ruling has been issued yet. Unless the court grants the injunction, the rule takes effect September 15 — replacing the 47-year-old open-ended duration of status framework with fixed four-year caps for F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors, and 240-day caps for I-visa journalists. Indian students, the largest international student cohort in the US, face the biggest impact, particularly PhD candidates whose programs exceed four years and those relying on OPT/STEM OPT pathways.
source: U.S. District Court, D. Mass. / Presidents' Alliance / NAFSA / PSBP Law

label: Sep 1, 2026
headline: 60-day grace period elimination clears OMB review — Federal Register publication imminent, public comment period to follow
summary: The DHS proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, E-1/E-2/E-3, and TN visa holders has cleared White House OMB review as of August 31, 2026. Publication in the Federal Register is expected imminently, after which a 30-to-60-day public comment period begins before DHS can finalize the rule. The proposal would return the system to the pre-2017 framework, under which job loss resulted in immediate loss of immigration status with no window to find a new sponsor, change status, or prepare to depart. The grace period — established by a 2016 DHS regulation effective January 2017 — has been a critical safeguard for foreign nationals navigating layoffs, corporate restructurings, and other employment disruptions. For Indian H-1B professionals, who make up over 70% of H-1B holders, the proposal would dramatically raise the stakes of any job loss, particularly during ongoing tech industry restructuring. The grace period remains in effect during the rulemaking process; the rule cannot be finalized until after the public comment period closes and DHS reviews all comments.
source: DHS / OMB-OIRA / Seyfarth Shaw / Mondaq

label: Aug 26, 2026
headline: State Department pauses immigrant visa interviews worldwide for public charge training — no timeline for resumption
summary: The U.S. State Department ordered a global pause on immigrant visa interviews at all embassies and consulates starting August 25, directing consular officers to undergo mandatory training on stricter public charge screening. Applicants with scheduled interviews are receiving cancellation emails with no new dates. The pause affects family-based and employment-based immigrant visa applicants processing through consulates abroad — not nonimmigrant visas (H-1B, student, tourist). The timing is significant: it came days after federal judges struck down the administration's 75-country blanket visa pause (Sayani v. Rubio on Aug 7, Judge Vargas' broader ruling on Aug 21) and a Diversity Visa pause (Judge Leon on Aug 25). Plaintiffs have filed emergency motions accusing the State Department of circumventing court orders. The department has not disclosed when interviews will resume, what the new training entails, or whether applicants retain their place in line. For Indian families in employment-based green card queues processing through consulates, the pause adds another delay on top of the EB-2/EB-5 Unavailable status. Diversity Visa applicants face a hard September 30 deadline that could erase their eligibility. Separately, the WSJ reported a pilot program requiring Dominican Republic immigrant visa applicants to post bonds of up to $250,000 — with plans to expand to other countries.
source: US State Department / USA TODAY / WSJ / Reuters / Ellis Immigration

label: Aug 25, 2026
headline: Trump administration plans largest mass visa revocation in US history — up to 200,000 B1/B2 holders who sought asylum targeted
summary: The State Department announced it is coordinating with DHS to revoke the B1 and B2 (business/tourist) visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who entered the US as short-term visitors but then filed for asylum. If carried out, it would be the largest single mass visa revocation in US history. The revocations target visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought or are currently seeking asylum. State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott confirmed the effort, though the revocations would not necessarily result in immediate deportation — most with pending asylum cases would be recategorized but lose their tourist/business status. The action follows the administration's broader crackdown: the State Department has already revoked more than 175,000 visas since Trump took office for his second term. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau alleged the immigration system 'has long been swamped by frivolous asylum claims.' While the measure primarily targets asylum seekers from Latin America, the Caribbean, and Africa, Indian nationals who entered on B1/B2 visas and subsequently filed asylum claims — a small but nonzero population — would also be affected. The move is expected to face legal challenges.
source: Associated Press / Reuters / State Department

label: Aug 24, 2026
headline: DHS publishes proposed rule to codify $103,265 H-1B fee through formal rulemaking — broader than struck-down executive order
summary: The Department of Homeland Security published a proposed rule in the Federal Register (DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0298, RIN 1615-AD20) to impose a $103,265 fee on all H-1B cap-subject petitions, including the 20,000 advanced-degree exemption. Unlike the original $100,000 Presidential Proclamation 10973 — vacated by a federal judge in June and left unenforceable by the First Circuit in July — the new proposal uses formal notice-and-comment rulemaking under INA §286(m), the fee statute courts cited as the proper authority. DHS estimates the fee would generate $8.8 billion annually from a projected 85,000 cap-subject petitions. Critically, the proposed rule is broader than the original executive order: it would cover F-1-to-H-1B transitions (previously exempt) and potentially renewals. Cap-exempt petitions (universities, nonprofits, research organizations), extensions, and employer transfers are excluded. The fee would be on top of all other existing fees. Public comments are due approximately 30 days after publication (~September 24). India's IT industry body Nasscom immediately responded, urging the US to weigh H-1B's role in addressing skill shortages. The rule could be finalized by end of year.
source: DHS / USCIS / Federal Register / Reuters / Nasscom

label: Aug 21, 2026
headline: September 2026 Visa Bulletin (final of FY2026): Zero employment-based movement for India — EB-2 and EB-5 still unavailable, family categories explode
summary: The State Department released the September 2026 Visa Bulletin — the final bulletin of fiscal year 2026 — revealing a stark split between family-sponsored and employment-based categories. Family-sponsored categories received a year-end number dump: F3 leaped 2 years 5 months, F4 gained 2 years 2 months, F1 advanced 13 months, F2B gained 20 months, and F2A moved to August 2026 (nearly current). Employment-based categories got virtually nothing: EB-1, EB-2, EB-3, and every EB-5 line are identical to August. India EB-2 and EB-5 Unreserved remain Unavailable, EB-1 India stays frozen at October 15, 2022, and EB-3 India remains stuck at January 1, 2014. Only EB-4 and Certain Religious Workers saw minor movement. The Dates for Filing chart for employment-based categories did not change by a single day. With FY2026 ending September 30, annual limits reset October 1 — the earliest point Indian EB-2 and EB-5 applicants could see visa numbers resume. USCIS also announced a revised Form I-485 effective September 18 (aligned with the public charge rule) with no grace period for using the old version.
source: US State Department / September 2026 Visa Bulletin (Vol. XI, No. 18)

label: Aug 17, 2026
headline: August visa wait times: Kolkata B1/B2 drops to 2 months (from 7), Hyderabad work/student visas surge to 5 months — mixed signals across India consulates
summary: The State Department's August 2026 wait time data reveals a dramatic reshuffling across India's consulates. Kolkata B1/B2 visitor visa wait plunged from 210 days (7 months) in July to just 60 days (2 months), making it the fastest in the country by far. Mumbai B1/B2 improved from 300 to 255 days (8.5 months). However, Hyderabad deteriorated sharply — B1/B2 rose to 315 days (10.5 months, now the longest), while work visa (H/L/O/P/Q) waits surged from ~45 days to 150 days and student visa (F/M/J) waits tripled from 45 to 135 days. New Delhi B1/B2 held at 255 days but student visas rose to 75 days. Chennai continues showing no interview availability — only dropbox processing (1-day turnaround). The Hyderabad surge across all categories may reflect operational constraints from the expanded social media vetting mandate that hit Indian consulates in December 2025.
source: US State Department / travel.state.gov / afnovisaguide.com

label: Aug 13, 2026
headline: BIA overrules 14-year precedent: advance parole travel now triggers 3- and 10-year unlawful-presence bars
summary: In Matter of Delcarmen-Lara (29 I&N Dec. 830, BIA 2026), the Board of Immigration Appeals held that leaving the US on advance parole counts as a 'departure' for purposes of the unlawful-presence bars under INA §212(a)(9)(B). The decision expressly overrules Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly (2012), a 14-year-old precedent that immigration lawyers and DACA/TPS/I-485 applicants had relied on to travel internationally without triggering the 3-year or 10-year reentry bars. Now, anyone who accumulated 180+ days of unlawful presence and then departs on advance parole may become inadmissible — requiring an I-601 waiver to reenter. The ruling applies prospectively (trips completed before August 13 are not affected), but immigration attorneys are issuing urgent warnings not to travel on advance parole without individual legal advice. While this most directly impacts DACA recipients and TPS holders, Indian green card applicants in the lengthy EB backlog who travel on advance parole while their I-485 is pending should also review their unlawful-presence history before any international travel.
source: BIA (Matter of Delcarmen-Lara) / Murthy Law Firm / Ogletree Deakins

label: Sep 2025
headline: Interview waiver eliminated for work & student visas
summary: H-1B, H-4, L-1, F-1, J-1, O-1 applicants no longer qualify for interview waiver. All must attend in-person interviews.
source: US State Department
